summary:
California is one of the states of the United States, and a trans visitor to California stands under the federal framework in every respect that touches documents, screening and admission. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. A traveller's passport can therefore mismatch their presentation, and trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Airport screening follows national rules. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy and can expose a traveller's trans status. Several foreign governments have responded to the document and data rules: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and by March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, had adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens. Visa decisions follow national rules as well. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking, and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody and care measures apply inside California like every other state. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people have reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups". On care, Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children", the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

California's own law runs against that current. Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 in September 2022, making California the first sanctuary state for transgender youth seeking medical care: out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers here, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care.

Recorded hostility in California is nonetheless the highest in the country. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, and California recorded the most of any state at 198, ahead of New Hampshire (72), Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50). Law-enforcement data for Los Angeles shows a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports over the same period, coinciding with Governor Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures.

Detention conditions in the state differ from federal practice. As of January 2021 California is the one state that allows transgender people to be housed in prison according to their gender identity, with identity-based housing inside the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented; in 2015 it became the first state to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation issued operational guidelines for transgender inmates. Federal policy returned to placement by sex assigned at birth after the January 2017 federal guidance was rescinded.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2026 analysis places California in the "Safest States" law band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, and argues that even the most protective statutory floors do not eliminate recorded hostility. That figure sits far below the 198 incidents the GLAAD ALERT Desk attributed to California for 2025, and the two counts are not reconciled by the sources; they appear to rest on different definitions of a counted incident.

The national pattern around facilities is uneven and moving against trans people in most states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Document rules elsewhere in the country are tightening faster than in California. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states.

Advocates have compared the December 2025 bounty instruction and the May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy, which stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist", to the early stages of genocide. In ICE custody, transgender men have reportedly been subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse.
localsOnly:
SB 107, signed in September 2022, makes California a sanctuary for transgender youth seeking medical care. Out-of-state minors can travel here for hormones and puberty blockers, and the statute shields their families from child-abuse investigations and from criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care, including against demands from other states.

Correctional policy is identity-based. California is the one state coded as allowing transgender inmates to be housed according to their gender identity, with placement inside the general population rather than in a separate unit, and no trans-only facility is documented. In 2015 the state became the first to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation issued operational guidelines covering care and housing for transgender inmates. Federal prisons operating in the state follow the national rule of placement by sex assigned at birth, which returned after the January 2017 federal guidance was rescinded.

Residents also live under the state's protective statutory band, scored 4.1 in a July 2026 analysis, alongside the highest recorded count of anti-LGBTQ incidents in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state California's current rules for changing the sex marker on a state driver's licence or birth certificate, so a visitor's state-issued identification position is not established here.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses whether California operates its own bathroom or facility-access restrictions for trans people in schools or public buildings, or how the federal single-sex facility ban applies to state-run buildings in California.

Unresolved: the discrepancy between the 1.9 incidents attributed to California by the July 2026 analysis and the 198 attributed by the GLAAD ALERT Desk for 2025 is not explained by either source, and the counting methodology behind each figure is not sourced.

Unresolved: the prison housing and surgery claims are dated January 2021 and 2015 respectively; no source in the inventory confirms that identity-based housing and funded surgery remain in effect after those dates, or describes how the 2026 federal Bureau of Prisons policy interacts with state-run facilities.

Not sourced: the inventory contains no California-specific hate-crime statute, charging data or conviction outcomes, only incident counts and a law-enforcement reporting trend for Los Angeles.
